accuracy.reason: All eight objectives accurately bound relational fit, null-sensitive constraints, ACID, statement snapshots, conditional-update concurrency, query access, WAL/replication and operational recovery. No automatic business correctness, all-standby freshness, universal CAP classification or historical durability guarantee. Primary followups substantiate claims beyond broad source pages.

evidence.quote: CHECK rejects values for which its expression is false. For required nonnegative stock, combine stock >= 0 with NOT NULL: a check alone does not reject a null result.

Synchronous settings wait for configured standby acknowledgements at a chosen stage. This trades commit latency and write availability for stronger protection; it does not make every standby instantly current.

mechanisms.reason: The last-unit example traces both observations, conditional decrement, wait/recheck, changed-row test and same-transaction order creation/rollback. This explains why a transaction alone is insufficient. Index filter/order diagram and old-replica state make query work and freshness limits concrete; transaction and rule diagrams are accurate within adjacent prose.

evidence.quote: Use a conditional update that decrements stock only while stock > 0, then check whether a row changed. Create the order only after a successful decrement in the same transaction; roll back both if required work fails. No row changed means no allocation.

At Read Committed, a competing update waits and rechecks its condition after the other update commits. MVCC reduces many reader/writer conflicts, but does not eliminate locks or retries. Stronger isolation can protect broader rules and can require retrying an aborted transaction.

coherence.reason: Client/server fit leads to declared rules, transaction boundary, competing updates, access paths, replica/failure costs and integrated design. Each card objective builds on definitions already supplied. Only PostgresDiagram applies here; its six rendered cases reinforce these mechanisms without adding unqualified guarantees.

evidence.quote: A transaction makes related database changes commit together or roll back together. ACID names four properties of that boundary.

Use keys and references for relationships, constraints for valid values and transactions for coupled changes. Protect concurrent decisions with conditional updates or appropriate locking and isolation.

decisions.reason: Explains embedded-storage alternative and primary write limits; weighs concurrency, indexes and replication costs; requires plans/measurements and explicit freshness/loss/latency/recovery targets. Connections, historical restores, exclusive failover authority and client routing are responsibilities rather than automatic benefits.

evidence.quote: For simple local storage, an embedded database can avoid a separate service. Requirements beyond one server's write capacity need further design; relational storage does not make PostgreSQL mandatory for every workload.

Specify stale-read tolerance, acceptable acknowledged-write loss and recovery targets before adding replicas. Choose acknowledgement and routing policies, safe failover and tested backups accordingly.

clarity.reason: Definitions are precise and concrete examples resolve the hardest concurrency and index concepts. The replication/CAP card compresses WAL, lag, acknowledgement stages, partition semantics and promotion into one card; sufficient but dense for the stated learner.

evidence.quote: Write-ahead logging (WAL) records changes for recovery before the corresponding changed data pages need to reach persistent storage. The primary accepts writes; a physical standby is a replica that receives and replays WAL to maintain its copy.
Promotion needs an eligible, sufficiently current standby, exclusive write authority and client routing. These policies determine behavior; a universal CP/AP label leaves them unexplained.

outcomes.reason: Actual learner covers client/server SQL, linked tables/joins/transactions, embedded/write-capacity alternatives, all five constraints with null semantics, concrete ID/reference/required-quantity mapping, rejected writes and cross-row/concurrency limits. All seven criteria and exact evidence checked.

Explains all ACID scopes and external-action exclusion; MVCC row versions and per-statement Read Committed; unsafe independent observations; conditional update with row-result test, same-transaction order creation, rollback and wait/recheck; locks/retries remain. All eight criteria satisfied by the taught solution, without needing an unprovided locking syntax.

Maps account/time query to candidate compound index, EXPLAIN and measurement, reasonable scans and maintenance cost. Defines WAL and primary/standby receive/replay, stale/lost-write windows, configurable synchronous stage costs, partition-time refusal and qualified promotion/authority/routing. All nine criteria supported; no streaming implementation detail is required beyond receiving/replaying changes.

Includes bounded connections, historical backups/restores, index/replica costs and primary write limit; integrates schema constraints, coupled stock/order transaction, conditional concurrency handling, query-plan validation and requirement-led read/ack/failover policy. Explicitly leaves unknown workload/recovery targets unresolved. All eight criteria follow exact slide evidence.

sourceChecks.claim: Tutorial concepts supports relational tables; https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-arch.html confirms separate client/server processes. Embedded alternative and write-limit caution are scoped design advice.

Constraint documentation confirms primary-key uniqueness/non-null, default UNIQUE null distinctions, nullable foreign references and CHECK true/null acceptance. Slide explicitly adds NOT NULL where absence is invalid.

Transaction tutorial confirms commit/rollback database boundary; isolation chapter and warm-standby settings support qualified isolation/durability. An HTTP side effect is outside that database boundary; backups retain a different historical capability.

Read Committed documentation confirms statement snapshots and waiting/rechecking the WHERE condition on an updated row; isolation failures require retry. Conditional stock decrement plus checked result and transactional order insertion is sound for the stated single-item rule.

Index introduction supports selective access and upkeep. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html and https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-ordering.html verify planner choice, ordered access and large-fraction scan tradeoff; no forced index use promised.

Warm standby supports WAL receipt/replay, async loss and configured synchronous stages/waits. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-intro.html confirms log-before-data-page persistence. Previously checked PostgreSQL failover and Brewer primary CAP sources support exclusive authority/routing and partition qualifications.

Continuous archiving supports historical recovery and retained logs. https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html documents resource-sensitive connection limits; index and standby docs support remaining costs. Restore-time testing is recommended validation, not a promised result.

Tutorial supplies relational foundation; design synthesis follows checked constraint, isolation, index, replication and recovery sources. No claimed measured throughput, universal product fit or automatic policy.
